richer media facilitate social perceptions and ability to evaluate expertise and deception, and that richer media can improve decision quality, particularly when participants have high levels of task-relevant knowledge and when they are not deceptive.
richer media facilitate decision quality when participants have high task-relevant knowledge and when deception is present in the decision environment.

the impacts of media richness on decision quality depend on the levels (high vs. low) of participant expertise and task-relevant knowledge and the levels (high, moderate, low, or none) of participant deception.

the impact of computer mediated communication systems on decision processes, decision outcomes, and decision quality.
the impact of computermediated communication systems on decision making and the role of social perceptions and communication clarity in this process.
understanding how computer-mediated communication systems can be used to enhance decision quality.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the richer the medium, the better the decision quality.
richer media are more appropriate than leaner media when participants have high levels of task-relevant knowledge and when there is a high level of deception among participants.

richer media facilitate social perceptions and perceived ability to judge others, which in turn facilitate communication clarity, which in turn facilitates decision quality when participants are experts and are not attempting to deceive others.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of richer media is beneficial when participants are highly knowledgeable about the decision problem, when they have a high level of trust and confidence in one another, and when they are able to evaluate one another's expertise and deception.
richer media can facilitate the development of a positive socio-emotional communication climate and the ability to evaluate others, which in turn, can facilitate decision quality.
richer media facilitate the development of a social context that can be used to make more informed decisions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of media richness are mediated through social perceptions and communication clarity.

media richness theory is a useful tool for understanding how computer-mediated communication systems affect decision quality and that richer media can be more effective than leaner media when participants' knowledge is high.
